title: Drop by drop (119–122)
hookLine: don't think lightly of evil or of good; drop by drop the water-pot fills (Dhammapada 121–122)

lines: A BUCKET UNDER A DRIPPING FAUCET.
cards: Put an empty bucket under a dripping faucet at bedtime. Drip. Nothing.
Drip. Still nothing, really, a film of water on the bottom. You go to sleep thinking it's not worth fixing.
In the morning the bucket is full, and maybe the floor is wet too. No single drop did that. Every drop did.

A lot of what shapes a life works like that faucet: one scroll, one snapped reply, one skipped walk, one small kindness. None of them seems to matter. Today the Dhammapada puts a water-pot in the rain.

teach.b: The verses start with something honest about timing. Verse one nineteen: "Even an evil-doer sees happiness as long as his evil deed has not ripened; but when his evil deed has ripened, then does the evil-doer see evil."

Verse one twenty says the same of a good person going through hard days. The image is fruit. Kamma ripening slowly came up with the milk that turns, khira; here the ripening gets its own word, vipāka.
So the text admits it plainly: people sometimes seem to get away with things, and good people sometimes suffer. Not yet ripe, the verses say. Then the twin verses of the water-pot.
Verse one twenty-one: "Let no man think lightly of evil, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled."
The fool, it goes on, fills up with harm, gathered little by little.

Verse one twenty-two says the same words about good, and ends: "the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little." A warning and a comfort, one sentence told twice. Small harms don't stay small.
And this week has been a small pot of its own. Birds in the sky that leave no trace. Calm thought, calm word.
One word of peace, sahassa, worth more than a thousand empty ones. The greatest conquest, over yourself. One day awake.

how: Buddhist teachers use the water-pot verses to encourage small daily merit, such as a little giving, a kept precept or a short sit, on the understanding that good and harm both build up gradually.

o: harm and good both build up, little by little
only big deeds really shape who you become
be patient: wait, and good things will come

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: the harm that hasn't ripened yet

s: the verses say small harms don't really count
"let no man think lightly of evil": drops fill the pot.
verses 121 and 122 use the same image, once for harm and once for good
a water-pot filled by falling drops, told twice.
verse 119 says wrongdoers are always unhappy right away
it admits they may see happiness until the deed has ripened.

games.q: you've told yourself one small lie a day for a month. it never caused trouble. what do the verses say about that?
o: the pot is filling, drop by drop.
games.why: "even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." the same works for good, gathered little by little.

practice: Picture an empty clay pot in front of you, and with each out-breath let one drop fall into it; don't count them, just watch.
Bring to mind one tiny good thing you could add today, like holding a door, putting your phone away at dinner, or a glass of water for someone: small on purpose, today's drop.
Then go back to the breath, and let the pot fill at its own pace.

wordCard.voice: Drop by drop. Verses one twenty-one and one twenty-two: a water-pot fills from falling drops, with harm or with good, little by little.

orig.note: Pali: a water-pot — udaka (water) and kumbha (pot), the jar that fills drop by drop.

carryVoice: Your line: drop by drop. Too small to count still counts. Day one hundred eighty-two, and a week complete.
